52.0.s.en: (1) The characteristics of the wicked man

52.0.0.en: 1- “Why boastest thou thyself in mischief, O mighty man? The goodness of God endureth continually.”

52.0.1.en: 1- Doeg the Edomite loved evil, practiced it and persisted in it. To win the favor of King Saul he committed many evils, such as lying; he held the lives of the priests cheap and killed them without pity, and even destroyed everyone in their city, women and children alike. He boasted that he did evil, and this is the first characteristic of the wicked man.

52.0.2.en: He represents ungodliness and is a type of the antichrist. The Holy Bible shows examples of such ungodly men who boast in evil, like Rabshakeh and Sennacherib.

52.0.3.en: 2- The mercy of God is every day: it halts the evil of the wicked, and it keeps and delivers the righteous, or promises them eternity, as happened with the priests of Nob (1 Sam 21). God, the Almighty, sets limits to evil by His mercy. Thus in this verse we see a contrast between the evils of man and the mercy of God, and this is the idea of the whole psalm.

52.1.0.en: 2- “Thy tongue deviseth mischiefs; like a sharp razor, working deceitfully.”

52.1.1.en: 1- The second characteristic in Doeg, or in the wicked man, is lying and devising mischiefs. He made Saul believe that Ahimelech was cooperating with David against Saul. So that Doeg might draw near to Saul, he lied to achieve his aim. He was also deceitful and a cheat: he joined the Jews and was circumcised. He did this and pretended, but in truth he did not love God and His worship, as the hardness of his heart shows, and his rush to kill the priests, whereas the true Jews, the servants of Saul, could not bring themselves to kill the priests.

52.1.2.en: 2- David likens Doeg to “a sharp razor,” which removes all the hair with ease, just as Doeg killed the priests and destroyed their city with ease. He thinks of evil, hastens to it and does it easily, because it is of his nature, and consequently he persists and goes on in it. In the same way a sharp razor wounds and cuts quickly anyone who is not careful of it; the wicked man is deceitful and cannot be trusted.

52.2.0.en: 3- “Thou lovest evil more than good; and lying rather than to speak righteousness. Selah.”

52.2.1.en: 1- The third characteristic of the wicked man is that he loves evil more than good. Doeg loved lying and inciting Saul against the priests more than finding an excuse for Ahimelech in helping David, for example that he did not know of any problems between David and Saul. In his love of evil Doeg used lying and hardness of heart, and slaughtered the priests.

52.2.2.en: 2- In the wicked man’s love of evil, he loved every evil word that destroys others and deceives them. The wicked man clings to the wicked and loves their evils, which makes him persist in his evils without limit.

52.2.3.en: 3- At the end of verse 3 we find the word “Selah,” which is a musical pause, so that man may contemplate the gravity of evil and keep away from it.

52.2.4.en: Take care lest the devil provoke you and you persist in any evil, however small or hidden from the eyes of people, for he wants to turn your heart to evil so as to separate you from God. When God warns you, hasten to repentance, so that you may regain your sonship to God, your nature may be purified, and you may return to doing good.

52.3.s.en: (2) The recompense of the wicked man

52.3.0.en: 5- “God shall likewise destroy thee for ever, he shall take thee away, and pluck thee out of thy dwelling place, and root thee out of the land of the living. Selah.”

52.3.1.en: 1- “Likewise” means therefore: as a result of the evil characteristics the wicked man held fast to, God brings many punishments upon him, namely:

52.3.2.en: a- He will destroy you: that is, God will shatter you and strip you of every show of your strength. This destruction lasts throughout his life, that is, for ever, so that he is cast into eternal torment.

52.3.3.en: b- He will take you away: the divine punishment comes suddenly. After God has been long-suffering toward the wicked man, who persisted in his evils for a long time, the divine punishment comes upon him suddenly and snatches him away from all his pleasures and his pride, and strips him of all ability and strength.

52.3.4.en: c- He will pluck you out of your dwelling place: however deeply rooted the wicked man is and however firmly he has established himself, and whatever power, connections or wealth he has, God plucks him out of his secure dwelling place, as a plant is plucked out of the ground, and casts him out to wither and be burned with fire. That is, he loses everything he built up for himself and is cast into the eternal fire.

52.3.5.en: d- He will root you out of the land of the living: the wicked man loses his life, either by death, or he is considered dead in the sight of God because he has separated himself from Him, and he has no place in the land of the living, that is, the Kingdom of Heaven. Because he rejected life with God on earth, he becomes dead for ever, that is, he does not feel God, and is tormented for ever, since the knowledge of God is life, and distance from Him is eternal torment.

52.3.6.en: 2- The verse ends with the word “Selah,” a musical pause for meditating on the punishment of the wicked man, so that man may keep away from evil.

52.4.0.en: 6- “The righteous also shall see, and fear, and shall laugh at him.” 7- “Lo, this is the man that made not God his strength; but trusted in the abundance of his riches, and strengthened himself in his wickedness.”

52.4.1.en: 1- When the righteous see the wicked man, who did not rely on God and did not make Him his stronghold, but trusted in his possessions and in his evil means by which he gains material things, and when the righteous see all this, they fear God. For they have grown accustomed to seeing God, so they feel His feelings and how His heart is grieved by evil. They fear for themselves lest they grow careless and fall into some of these evils, and so they become more watchful and careful, always remembering the fear of God.

52.4.2.en: 2- The righteous also laugh at evil, that is, they scorn it and feel that it is a bad, trivial and passing thing, so it does not entice them to do it, but they loathe it, and their clinging to God increases.

52.4.3.en: Remember the fear of God at all times, so that it may keep you from sin and bring you near to God, and you will enjoy seeing Him, and He will even reveal to you the treasures of His knowledge, and you will rejoice in fellowship with Him.

52.5.s.en: (3) The conduct of the righteous man and his reward

52.5.0.en: 8- “But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God: I trust in the mercy of God for ever and ever.”

52.5.1.en: 1- When the righteous man sees the sins of the wicked man, he keeps away from him; this is the negative side. But on the positive side, the righteous man enjoys, as he expresses in this verse, the following:

52.5.2.en: a- He likens himself to a green olive tree, that is, a tree that bears fruit, because the spiritual man has spiritual fruits. It also produces the oil that the believer needs to fill his lamp, and this oil is good works. The olive tree is green, that is, full of life through God who works in it. The olive tree also signifies peace, as in the story of Noah, because the righteous man makes peace and inclines to it, and God fills his heart with peace.

52.5.3.en: b- “In the house of God”: the secret of the strength of this olive tree is that it is planted in the house of God, that is, it has a very strong relationship, deeply rooted in the worship of God, and so it receives all the blessings mentioned before, and no one can pluck it up; that is, the wicked and all their sins do not affect it.

52.5.4.en: 2- The steadfastness of the righteous man depends on his trust in God, who establishes him, keeps him, defends him and blesses him in this life and then in eternity.

52.5.5.en: 3- David likens himself to the olive tree planted in the house of God, though he was driven out and excluded from the house of God, because his heart was attached to God and to His house. For this reason we read this part of the psalm on the eve of the feast of St. John the Baptist (2 Thout), who lived in the wilderness, driven out by Herod, yet whose heart was attached to the house of the Lord and to His Christ more than all the people of the Jews.

52.5.6.en: 4- The green olive tree signifies Christ, for all the meanings mentioned above are fulfilled in Christ.

52.6.0.en: 9- “I will praise thee for ever, because thou hast done it: and I will wait on thy name; for it is good before thy saints.”

52.6.1.en: 1- At the end of the psalm David thanks God and praises Him, because He has given him the blessings mentioned in this psalm. This is God’s work in him; he appreciates the work of God and thanks Him, and so he remains in a deep relationship and constant love for God.

52.6.2.en: 2- This praise produced in David’s heart longings toward God, which he expresses by saying that he waits on the Lord, that is, he hungers and thirsts for God, and God gives him blessings and joy in Him. As David’s life is enlightened, he becomes an example to God’s saints, who also wait on the Lord, and they are encouraged in their striving toward God. In David’s waiting on God’s name he bears the toils of life and the devil’s wars with joy, confident of God’s support for him and of the blessings He will give him, because those who believe in God are exposed to many wars, and God permits them, but at the same time He grants His children patience and support, and even more than this, the experience of His fellowship in the midst of tribulations.

52.6.3.en: Your trust in God gives you support and steadfastness in your spiritual life, so do not be troubled by the changes of life or the devil’s wars, and continue in your spiritual growth.

52.6.4.en: The salvation of the Lord. A psalm of David when he fled from the face of Absalom his son: “LORD, how are they increased that trouble me!” (v. 1) Introduction:

52.6.5.en: a- This psalm is a repetition of Psalm 14, but why is this psalm repeated in a single book?

52.6.6.en: 1- Because their writer is one, David the prophet, they are very similar.

52.6.7.en: 2- The first psalm, which is Psalm 14, was placed in the first group according to the Jewish division, which includes (Ps 1-41), the group that speaks of the salvation of the individual; it shows the turning aside of man’s heart after evil, and for this reason Christ became incarnate to redeem him. The second psalm (Ps 53) was placed in the second group, which includes (Ps 42-72), the group that speaks of the salvation of the community, or the Church, which as a whole is exposed to turning aside and corruption, and all of which needs salvation.

52.6.8.en: 3- The idea of this psalm, that man’s heart is exposed to corruption, evil and betrayal, is an idea repeated throughout the generations. The purpose of the repetition is to alert man to the gravity of this corruption so that he may guard against it, especially since every man, however near to God, is exposed to falling, as happened with Judas, the disciple of Christ.

52.6.9.en: 4- Despite the repetition of the psalm, there are some differences between the two psalms, and this confirms that the writer wrote each of them separately, so the writing comes out slightly different and not an exact copy; this psalm is not a copy of the other psalm. This confirms that the Holy Bible has not been corrupted: the hand of man did not interfere to delete one of these psalms so that no one would object to this repetition.

52.6.10.en: b- The differences between the two psalms:

52.6.11.en: 1- In (Ps 14:1) we find “they have done abominable works,” while in (Ps 53:1) we find instead “have done abominable iniquity.”

52.6.12.en: 2- In (Ps 14:2) we find “The LORD looked down from heaven,” while in (Ps 53:2) we find instead “God looked down from heaven.”

52.6.13.en: 3- In (Ps 14:3) we find “They are all gone aside,” while in (Ps 53:3) we find instead “Every one of them is gone back.”

52.6.14.en: 4- In (Ps 14:4) we find “Have all the workers of iniquity no knowledge?” while in (Ps 53:4) we find instead “Have the workers of iniquity no knowledge?”

52.6.15.en: 5- (Ps 14:5, 6) tells us of the fear of the wicked toward the righteous, despite their opposing and resisting them and the humble man, as we explained in detail in (Ps 14). But (Ps 53:5) speaks of the fear of the wicked where there was nothing to fear, and God scattered the strength of those who besieged the righteous man and put them to shame, because they are wicked and God has rejected them, as He removed the strength of Sennacherib and his army, who besieged Jerusalem in the days of King Hezekiah. That is, (Ps 53:5) is a merging of the meaning of verses (5, 6) in (Ps 14).

52.6.16.en: 6- We notice that the numbering differs after this between the two psalms, that is, (Ps 14:7) corresponds to (Ps 53:6). The certainty of divine salvation. A poem of David when the Ziphims came and said to Saul, Doth not David hide himself with us? “Save me, O God, by thy name” (v. 1) Introduction:

52.6.17.en: 1- Its writer: David, as mentioned in the title.

52.6.19.en: When David was driven out by Saul and reached the hill country of Ziph, which lies in the tribe of Judah south of Jerusalem and Hebron. The Ziphites went to Saul and told him that David was hiding with them, so that he might come and seize him. This shows the extent of their fear of Saul and their attempt to please him, but God rescued him from Saul’s hand, and the Ziphites tried again and told Saul that David was in the wilderness of Ziph, and God rescued him again (1 Sam 26:1-25). Most likely David wrote this psalm after God’s first rescue of him, when he was in En-gedi and Saul had besieged him and was about to seize him, but news came to him of the Philistines’ raid on the land of the children of Israel, so he left David and went to face the Philistines (1 Sam 23:41-29). So David thanked God, who allowed this raid in order to rescue him from Saul’s hand.

52.6.20.en: 3- In this psalm David asks God to save him, and God intervenes and saves him, so he thanks Him for his salvation and praises Him. It is a psalm of thanksgiving for everyone who has passed through tribulation and prayed to God, and He delivered him.

52.6.21.en: 4- It is one of the eight psalms whose titles say that David was driven out by Saul, and they are called the psalms of the fugitive.

52.6.22.en: 5- This psalm completes the psalm before it, because Psalm 53 shows the resistance of the wicked to the righteous man, and this psalm shows God’s support for the righteous man and His rescuing him from the hands of the wicked.

52.6.23.en: 6- This psalm is found at the beginning of the prayer of the Sixth Hour in the Agpeya, the hour in which Christ is crucified for the world, and David suffers pains and shares Christ’s cross, then offers the sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving to God; that is, we glorify the sacrifice of Christ on the cross with thanksgiving and praise. Therefore the Western Church reads it on Great Friday in remembrance of the crucifixion of Christ.

54.0.0.en: 1- “Save me, O God, by thy name, and judge me by thy strength.”

54.0.1.en: 1- The name of God saves His children and breaks His enemies. Therefore the Church has cared to repeat the name of God since the first centuries of Christianity, in the Jesus Prayer and also in the daily psalis of the Midnight Praise.

54.0.2.en: 2- Because David walks in uprightness, he asks for God’s just judgment to rescue him from his enemies. He trusts in God’s justice and in his own (David’s) upright conduct, and believes that God does not reject the prayers of those who seek Him; therefore the Church asks Christ, her Savior, whatever tribulations befall her, confident of His power and protection.

54.1.0.en: 2- “Hear my prayer, O God; give ear to the words of my mouth.”

54.1.1.en: David prays from his heart without words, and opens his lips with audible prayers; with his heart and his tongue he asks God to rescue him from his enemies. Of course God cannot leave him.

54.2.0.en: 3- “For strangers are risen up against me, and oppressors seek after my soul: they have not set God before them. Selah.”

54.2.1.en: 1- David divides his enemies into two groups:

54.2.2.en: a- Strangers: by them he means the Ziphites, though they are Jews and of his own tribe, the tribe of Judah, but they became strangers to him and did not love him, and tried to kill him by delivering him into Saul’s hand.

54.2.3.en: b- The oppressors: by them he means Saul and his soldiers, who wanted to kill David and tried to do so many times.

54.2.4.en: These two groups did evil because they disregarded the existence of God, so there was nothing within them but their own evil human thoughts, but God is able to rescue David from their hands.

54.2.5.en: 2- The Church meets enemies in every generation, whether from her own children who have become strangers to her by falling into heresies, or pride, or various lusts, and sometimes strangers who are not children of the Church. These seek the help of the strong ones of the world to harm the Church, and they have no fear of God before them, but the mighty God rescues His Church however much the wicked increase against her.

54.2.6.en: 3- This verse ends with the word “Selah,” a musical pause for meditating on the name of God, who keeps us, protects us, strengthens us and satisfies our souls.

54.2.7.en: Do not fear the wicked and their threats, however strong or many they are, because God is able to protect you. Only seek God and press upon Him, and you will obtain His mercies and blessings.

54.3.0.en: 4- “Behold, God is mine helper: the Lord is with them that uphold my soul.”

54.3.1.en: 1- Although David began the psalm by asking God for salvation, he returns to thank God who supports him and to praise Him, and this is David’s habit in all his psalms. Here he declares that the Lord is his helper, even his supporter; therefore, if God is helper and upholder, who can stand against David? This shows David’s faith and his peace of mind in God’s hands.

54.3.2.en: 2- And when he says that the Lord is with them that uphold his soul, he does not mean that He is merely one of the supporters, but that He is the true, principal supporter, even if there were some people supporting David. In addition, God’s presence among the supporters encourages these supporters in their support of David.

54.4.0.en: 5- “He shall reward evil unto mine enemies: cut them off in thy truth.”

54.4.1.en: 1- In the spirit of prophecy David foretells of his enemies that their evil will return upon their own heads, and that by God’s truth, that is, His power, these enemies will be cut off. In this the divine justice is established, and the righteous are not troubled by the abundance of evil. Perhaps the remaining wicked will repent and believe in God.

54.4.2.en: 2- By the enemies he may mean the demons, whose end is eternal torment.

54.4.3.en: 3- David does not mean vengeance or gloating over his enemies, for David’s forgiveness is clear, since he pardoned Saul his enemy twice, though he was able to destroy him. So of course here he does not mean to take vengeance on his enemies, but to show the corruption and futility of evil.

54.5.0.en: 6- “I will freely sacrifice unto thee: I will praise thy name, O LORD; for it is good.”

54.5.1.en: Freely: willingly, and of good will.

54.5.2.en: 1- Since David believed in God, his helper and supporter and Deliverer from all his tribulations, his heart was moved with love toward God to offer Him sacrifices of thanksgiving as an expression of his love, and not to seek a reward, for he had already received peace of mind and peace through God’s support for him. These sacrifices are not obligatory for David but freewill, out of love from him, because David was excluded and driven out, far from the Temple, and could not offer animal sacrifices, so he offered the freewill sacrifices of the lips, as praise to God. What moves David to thank God is his constant contemplation of God’s goodness, care and continual gifts to him.

54.6.0.en: 7- “For he hath delivered me out of all trouble: and mine eye hath seen his desire upon mine enemies.”

54.6.1.en: 1- God’s goodness appeared plainly in rescuing David from every tribulation, and even in God’s swift intervention in striking the enemies, so David saw his victory and was encouraged to stand firm in his righteousness. Therefore he continued to thank and praise God, for he always recalled what his eyes had seen of God’s works with him and His rescue of him from the enemies.

54.6.2.en: 2- It may be that God granted David a vision of the defeat of his enemies, or their eternal destruction, so that he would not be troubled by them; therefore he was encouraged and stood firm in his faith and thanksgiving.

54.6.3.en: Look to Christ, your God and Savior, and your heart will be encouraged before any difficult circumstances; you will even become brave, fearing no one, and enjoy the experience of God, so that you praise Him always.

54.6.4.en: God saves those who trust in Him. To the chief Musician on stringed instruments. A poem of David: “Give ear to my prayer, O God; and hide not thyself from my supplication” (v. 1) Introduction:

54.6.7.en: When David was fleeing from the face of Absalom his son; for Absalom kept stirring up the city of Jerusalem against his father for two years and winning the people over to himself. Then he went to Hebron, gathered an army and attacked Jerusalem, and David fled lest his son Absalom kill him, by the counsel of Ahithophel, who was one of David’s greatest counselors and betrayed him and joined Absalom, and devised a plot to drive David out and then kill him (2 Sam 15:7-13).

54.6.8.en: 3- This psalm, as the title indicates, was sung to the accompaniment of stringed instruments, which are musical instruments with strings, each of which has a single string.

54.6.9.en: 4- This psalm resembles Psalm (41) in that both speak of the betrayal of a friend.

54.6.10.en: 5- Because this psalm speaks of the betrayal of a friend, it is a prophecy about Jeremiah and the betrayal of his family and those who loved him (Jer 12:6), and also a prophecy about the betrayal of Christ by Judas Iscariot (Mt 26:14).

54.6.11.en: 6- This psalm is not found in the prayers of the Agpeya.
